title: The Actor Model for Agents — Async Messages and Typed Runtimes
service: ActorRT: a stdlib actor runtime after AutoGen v0.4 Core (send only queues, deep-copied messages, a per-handler outbox, a dead-letter queue, topic subscriptions), with the lesson's reviewer and checklist, a binary inbox journal, round-robin and selector group chats on the runtime, length-prefixed frames to actors on another host, and spawn trees with cascading stop

parts.lesson_anchor: Actors (private state, inbox, handler; two actors cannot share memory); Why decoupling matters (v0.2's agent_a.chat(agent_b) blocks agent_a until agent_b returns, while v0.4's send(agent_b, msg) puts the message in agent_b's inbox and returns and the runtime delivers later; fault isolation: the runtime catches the failure in B's handler and dead-letters it); Core layer Topic and Key Terms: Topic (named publish-subscribe route); code/main.py Runtime.send, run_until_idle and ChecklistAgent; quiz Q3, Q9, Q11 and Q13
planted_bugs: Runtime.send called inside a handler calls the recipient's receive at once, the v0.2 agent_a.chat(agent_b) way, instead of queuing: the reviewer's TypeError for a snippet that is not text runs up into the checklist's start handler and is dead-lettered against the start message, while the review itself never reaches the dead-letter queue and the snippets after it are never sent; it is raised in ReviewerAgent.receive and caught in run_until_idle, one handler away from the root cause in send
a handler's sends are queued at once, so a batch that fails after forwarding gamma still delivers it (quiz Q11.2)
ChecklistAgent declares consensus True while the verdicts that have arrived are ok, and waits for a hard-coded 3 (quiz Q9)
subscribe dedups against one list of (topic, name) pairs and publish scans every subscription
parts.timing_assert: 8000 subscriptions and 20000 publishes under 0.1 s; the list scan takes 1.3 to 3.4 s on this machine (1.3 to 1.6 s when it is quiet), the topic index 2.6 to 9.1 ms; an index for publish with subscribe still scanning the list takes 0.24 to 0.28 s
parts.overfix_guard: send only queues: a try/except around the direct call keeps the dead letter right but still runs the reviewer inside the checklist's handler (a run with max_messages=1 handles both reviews), and catching then re-raising or swallowing gets the dead letters wrong; delivery keeps the order of sending (a newest-first queue, or a handler's messages put ahead of the waiting mail, fails); the deep copy, which the starter already makes, stays guarded: taken when send() is called (the caller appends to its list afterwards and Batcher reuses its buffer, so copies at delivery or at commit fail), one per recipient (one shared copy per publish fails), deep (copy.copy fails) and not dropped once delivery waits for the queue (audit's KeyError: 'id'); dropping is per handler call (clearing the queue by sender or by mid loses the reviewer's queued verdicts and the alpha and beta of the call that returned); the outbox resets after a failure; the index keeps first-subscription order and dedups (set and list fail)

deviations: Part 1 timing: the suggested list.pop(0) queue cannot meet the 8x margin on both sides. Measured on this machine, a bare pop loop over 60000 queued messages is only 37x slower than a deque (0.33 s against 8.8 ms) and 64x at 120000 (1.37 s), and the runtime's own per-message work would cut that to about 10x to 20x. The quadratic defect is the lesson's Topic instead: subscribe dedups against one list of pairs and publish scans every subscription. The starter's queue is a deque, as in the lesson code.

Part 1 symptom: the reviewer raises on a snippet that is not text, so with send delivering synchronously inside a handler the error surfaces as a dead letter against the checklist's start message, one handler away from send. The reviewer publishes each verdict on the reviews topic, heard by the checklist and an audit actor; the checklist sends {id, code} reviews, keeps verdicts by index, pops the id and sorts the issues, so the per-recipient deep copy, which the starter already makes, is guarded by audit's KeyError: 'id'. The main assertions are whom a dead letter is charged to and that one actor's failure leaves the other actors' work intact, plus a one-message run that leaves the reviews in the inbox; the order of handling is only a side check.

Part 2: the record header is binary (a kind byte, an 8-byte mid, a 4-byte length) and the payload depends on the kind (JSON for M, nothing for A, UTF-8 text for D), so the file differs from the Part 4 frames; the exactness also covers recovery itself: what is written when (M at commit, A after the handler's own messages, D on dead-lettering), a crash inside a handler simulated with a BaseException, a torn tail cut back, and the next mid taken from the whole journal.

Part 3: the team is itself the manager actor and talks to participants only with speak and said messages. The selector also picks the first turn, every turn records a reason (rotation, selector, unknown, repeat), and a chat that goes idle before it stops is stalled. The stop word and max_messages rules are this exam's, documented in teams.py; the lesson only describes a fixed rotation and a selector that picks the next speaker from context.

Part 4: a Link registers a RemoteActor stand-in for each actor on the other host, so the unchanged checklist and reviewer run across two hosts. serve() is an async generator; added a zero-length heartbeat frame, frames already waiting sent before the first read, mids of the receiving host, and an audit proxy on the far side so one delivery writes two frames.

Part 5: spawn, stop and tree are Runtime methods. The stop order is post-order with the most recently spawned child first, and the tree grows through messages so that spawn order differs from pre-order and a reverse-spawn-order stop fails.
